related.title: Trump lashes out at NATO as first day of summit wraps in Turkiye
related.summary: Russia-Ukraine war Also on the summit’s agenda is NATO’s military support for Ukraine, as President Volodymyr Zelenskyy urges the alliance to step up aid for the country’s air defences. United States President Donald Trump has declared he is “very disappointed with NATO” on the first day of a summit of leaders of the mutual defence alliance in Turkiye that exposed tensions over European defence spending, the Russia-Ukraine war and the future of Greenland.
bullets: Russia-Ukraine war Also on the summit’s agenda is NATO’s military support for Ukraine, as President Volodymyr Zelenskyy urges the alliance to step up aid for the country’s air defences.

United States President Donald Trump has declared he is “very disappointed with NATO” on the first day of a summit of leaders of the mutual defence alliance in Turkiye that exposed tensions over European defence spending, the Russia-Ukraine war and the future of Greenland.

“It’s too bad it took so long, but I think something’s going to come out.” Norway says it would provide three billion Norwegian crowns ($306.2m) for Ukraine’s air defence, specifically to protect against ballistic missiles, while Europe and Canada are expected to pledge to keep military support flowing to Ukraine in 2026 and 2027 at the summit.

After criticising NATO allies during a news conference with Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, Trump said that if the summit “weren’t held in Turkiye, where my friend happens to be a very strong leader, a very strong person, it’s possible that I wouldn’t have attended”.

related.title: Recession off the cards but Australia faces dreary outlook, economists say
related.summary: Belinda Allen, CBA’s head of Australian economics, said she had never thought a recession was likely, but that “the impact of the war on energy markets and the economy were less severe than we had anticipated”. The de-escalation of the Middle East conflict has been accompanied by a major retreat in global oil prices back to prewar levels, essentially removing the worst-case scenarios contemplated before Donald Trump’s wobbly ceasefire with Iran was announced in mid-June.

Fears of a recession have fallen away, with economists saying that Australia is set to safely navigate the biggest global oil supply shock in history even as they warn of sub-standard growth in the year ahead.
“We think no more [Reserve Bank] interest rate hikes are needed, but we still see some lingering risks there,” Allen said.
